turns.speaker: Cody
turns.text: What the product looks like today is you open the app and you can find a space to leave your things all over the city. So the goal is on every block of the city.

turns.speaker: Nicole
turns.text: So like a storage solution?

turns.speaker: Cody
turns.text: Yeah, that's right. So a lot of travelers will use us to store their luggage. A lot of folks will use us before going to, say, an event at Madison Square Garden. All kinds of use cases.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So..

turns.speaker: Nicole
turns.text: Sorry Is it sharing economy? Or are you using…

turns.speaker: Cody
turns.text: Yeah, so we’re storing things in small businesses that have extra space. We have 65 store locations between New York City and San Francisco.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: So it’s a storage app? A storage company? You’re enabling people to store things temporarily?

turns.speaker: Cody
turns.text: That’s right.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: And tell us about the business model. What kind of revenue are you generating? How does it all work?

turns.speaker: Cody
turns.text: So there’s two value props for the stores. One is extra foot traffic. Our customers, we estimate more than half of them buy from our small business partners. The second value prop is we do a revenue share with them. So basically we charge $6 per bag per day with the current model, and we give $3 now phasing that to $2 per bag to the store partners. So they win on both of those value props.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: And is the $6 charge regardless of the size of the item?

turns.speaker: Cody
turns.text: That’s right. As long as you can pick it up with two hands. So we do backpacks, suitcases, work bags, gym bags, all kinds of things.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: How long have you been doing this for?

turns.speaker: Cody
turns.text: We started last October.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Ok. And how fast are you scaling on revenue? What’s going on?

turns.speaker: Cody
turns.text: So basically we’ve been in product development mode, came out of that in February, and since then we’ve been growing 50% month over month. So last month we did $8,500 in revenue.

turns.speaker: Cody
turns.text: So in addition to the money, one of the things we’re looking for in this investment around is partnerships. So folks who have a lot of retail connections and they can help us flip some of these connections really, really fast.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Yeah. Like a chain.

turns.speaker: Cody
turns.text: If we could get one of these big guys…

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: I’m not convinced a big retailer is going to do this with you. I think it’s the Ma and Pa stores that don’t have to go through... I mean the amount of stuff that you’re going to have to go through, in insurance and probably with a 7Eleven is just, I don’t know, I’d be shocked if they would do it.

turns.speaker: Nicole
turns.text: It's going to be an 18 month long sales cycle.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: You're telling me a big chain is signing you up?

turns.speaker: Cody
turns.text: We actually had Kmart reach out to us and say, hey, we're interested.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Kmart?

turns.speaker: Cody
turns.text: Yeah. Brick and mortar is dying.

turns.speaker: Nicole
turns.text: They’re still alive?

turns.speaker: Cody
turns.text: They’re losing all their customers. And so they’re desperate for traffic. So they come to us and UPS. They have all kinds of add-on services, like passport photos, and fingerprinting services. They’re looking for these add-on businesses.

turns.speaker: Nicole
turns.text: You like it.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: I do like it.

turns.speaker: Nicole
turns.text: I know you do.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: I like it.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I actually do too. I’m killing myself here.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: I like him. And I like it. Like this is one of these things where...

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: You want to go in, don't you?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I want to go in.

turns.speaker: Michael
turns.text: Yeah, don't you? I know you do. I know you're changing your mind.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I am. You know one person said to me that the businesses that you roll your eyes at right? are the ones that ultimately are the best. The people that have uh the most ridiculous ideas are the ones you should pay attention to the most. Um Ergo, Airbnb and all those others. I’m going to reverse because everything we’ve brought up, everything that we’ve hit you with you’ve seen all these different issues. I’m going to go in for $100,000.
